mcq_picks.reasoning: The title page advertises a description of the country, its commodities, people, government, and religion — practical knowledge for settlers, not a story of conquest and treasure. A claims gold the page never mentions; C invents a viceroy; D invents Native agreement.

'Taken faithfully as they were written' is a claim to a trustworthy record, aimed at drawing settlers and investors. A is the opposite of the book's purpose; B invents a Spanish demand; C invents a profit claim.

A 1612 printed book selling Virginia to English readers illustrates the shift from exploration to permanent settlement backed by print. B is false (the Armada did not end Spanish claims); C is false (the crown did not rule Virginia directly); D is false (no single-generation replacement).
Walls, cannons, storehouses and dwellings = a fortified trading post holding goods and defending the fur trade. Not a farming town (A), not only a mission (B), not a palace (D).

The fur trade needed few settlers and relied on Native partners, so a small river post served France better than farms. B is false (France had ships — Champlain sailed); C is false (no royal ban); D is nonsense (rich soil would invite farming, not emptiness).

One small post on a great river shows a vast claim held by very few settlers, so France had to rely on Native allies and trade rather than numbers. A overstates control; B contradicts the fur-trade partnership; C is false (Quebec was tiny).

The excerpt's own words — 'covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil Body Politick' — are a promise to bind into one body governing itself by laws they made together. A invents a church requirement; B contradicts 'Loyal Subjects of our dread Sovereign Lord King James'; D invents land division.
The Compact created government by the settlers' own agreement, unlike Spanish rule imposed by the crown. A is backwards; C invents a fur monopoly; D invents an encomienda.
They anchored at Cape Cod, outside the land their patent covered, so they agreed to govern themselves before going ashore. B, C and D invent a sermon, a Spanish demand, and a fur-trade promise.

The Compact promises government by agreement and says nothing about religious freedom; the Puritan colonies later banished Williams and Hutchinson for their beliefs. A is false (no list of individual rights); B is false (no voting promise); C is false (they remain the king's loyal subjects).

'The eyes of all people are upon us' — the world will be watching, so the settlers must live up to the godly community they claim. A invents conquest; C mistakes a metaphor for a fort; D invents trade.

Winthrop preached aboard the Arbella in 1630 as the settlers sailed to found Massachusetts Bay. A names the wrong ship and year; B gets the timing backwards (preached before landing); D names the wrong speaker.

The vision claims the world will watch, but the colony banished Williams and Hutchinson for dissenting from its church — the limit of the vision. B and C invent trade and military claims; D is false (Winthrop, a colonial governor, wrote it).

Few Frenchmen, mostly single men, could not work the fur trade alone — France relied on Native partners and allies. A is false (France did not abandon New France); B is false (few settlers made Native peoples more, not less, important); D is false (no plantation/slave system in New France).

The table shows Jamestown's tiny, dying company venture of men seeking profit against Massachusetts Bay's 20,000+ settlers. A is false (different companies and purposes); B is false (Massachusetts Bay did not lose most settlers); C is false (not a handful of families).

James created the Dominion by revoking charters and placing the colonies under one royal governor — the crown could revoke charters and rule directly. B is false (no Parliamentary approval needed); C is false (colonies resisted); D is false (the Burgesses predated the Dominion by decades).
An assembly with settlers choosing men to make laws was a lure for settlers — a voice in their own laws. A is false; C is false (the king did not rule through it); D is false (the governor stayed).

The Burgesses survived the change to royal rule because elected assemblies were already rooted in colonial life. A is false (the king did take an interest); B overstates (not more powerful than the king); D is false (the company was dissolved).

Hakluyt's 'idle poor' points to enclosure and population growth leaving English people without land or work. The Armada (A) and Ireland (C) do not explain idle poor; D is not in the passage and not the driver.

Hakluyt pairs trade goods with spreading Protestantism against Catholic Spain — both a commercial venture and a religious challenge. B ignores the trade half; C is false (not a royal project); D is false (not a copy of Spain's conquest empire).
The table lists Virginia's main reason as economic gain (tobacco). Direct table read.

The table's reasons — company, proprietors, religious groups — show private companies, proprietors, and religious groups did the founding. A is false (the king did not found them all); C is false (reasons differ); D is false (Pennsylvania 1682, Georgia 1732).

Maryland and Pennsylvania as refuges show the charter system let different religious minorities build their own refuges. A is false (different groups); B is false (neither banned all other religions); C is false (not founded by the king).
The passage states Georgia was meant as a buffer between Spanish Florida and South Carolina. Direct passage read.
Small land grants and no slavery were meant to keep Georgia a colony of small farmers, not plantations — armed small farmers defending the buffer. A is the opposite; B and D invent motives.

Both founding rules were gone by 1751 because colonists' economic interests overturned the trustees' design. A is false (the trustees did want success); C is false (Spain did not conquer Georgia); D is false (the king did not forbid the trustees' rules).
The passage says the Acts stayed on the books but few customs officers enforced them — enforcement changed, not the law. Direct passage read; A, C and D all contradict it.

By elimination: A is false (no independence in 1721); B is false (trade with England continued); C is false (Walpole did not believe in colonial nationhood). D — distance, other wars, Walpole's priorities — is the only surviving explanation. Note: the stimulus itself states only the fact of neglect, not the reason; the reason must be taught in the lesson for this item to be fully fair.
